title: Xanthus (the river Scamander)
greek: Ξάνθου δινήεντος, ὃν ἀθάνατος τέκετο Ζεύς (Xanthou dinēentos, hon athanatos teketo Zeus)
short: The river of Troy has two names: the gods call him Xanthus ('Tawny'), men call him Scamander. In this book the river becomes a combatant.
body: Book 20 has already told us the double name: the river 'whom gods call Xanthus, but men Scamander' (Il. 20.74). Xanthos means 'yellow, tawny', probably from the colour of its silt-laden water. Rivers in Homer are gods and sons of Zeus, the sky-god whose rain feeds them; hence the formula 'that immortal Zeus begat' and the epithet 'heaven-fed' later in the book (21.268, 326). Walter Leaf observes that the ford named here appears only in this same formal couplet (14.433-4, 24.692-3) and may be a poetic convenience rather than a fixed point of Trojan topography. Gregory Nagy describes the strategic picture: so long as Akhilleus held aloof the Trojans kept the ground on their side of the river facing the Achaeans; now they are pushed back to its edge, and many die in the water. The choice of the divine name Xanthus at the opening prepares the extraordinary episode in which the river rises against Akhilleus (21.211-382). Akhilleus' later boast that the seed of Zeus is stronger than the seed of rivers (21.190-1) is a direct provocation to this god.

title: The locust simile
greek: ὡς δ' ὅθ' ὑπὸ ῥιπῆς πυρὸς ἀκρίδες ἠερέθονται (hōs d' hoth' hupo rhipēs puros akrides ēerethontai)
short: The fleeing Trojans are like locusts driven into a river by fire: Akhilleus is the fire, and the image foreshadows the clash of fire and water later in the book.
body: The Trojans plunge into the river 'as when beneath the rush of fire locusts take wing' and shrink down into the water. Walter Leaf records that the scholia call this way of fighting locusts characteristic of Cyprus, where it was still used in his own day, and that Strabo describes the same method among the 'locust-eaters' of Ethiopia (Strabo 16.4.12). The simile works on two levels. It shrinks the Trojans to swarming insects, a measure of how far beyond ordinary scale Akhilleus' slaughter has gone. It also sets up the elemental pattern of the whole book: Akhilleus is fire, the Trojans seek refuge in water, and later Hephaestus will literally turn fire against the river (21.342-382), as Gregory Nagy stresses in his reading of the fire-water conflict. Similes from farming and pest control recur in this book (compare the irrigation simile at 21.257-62), setting a peaceful, practical world against the violence of the battle.

title: The dolphin simile (and a gap in this text)
greek: ὡς δ' ὑπὸ δελφῖνος μεγακήτεος ἰχθύες ἄλλοι (hōs d' hupo delphinos megakēteos ikhthues alloi)
short: The Trojans cower like small fish fleeing a huge dolphin into the corners of a harbour. Part of this simile is missing from the text here.
body: Read carefully: between 'as they were' and 'anchorage in their terror' some words of the translation are missing in this copy. The Greek (21.20-24) says that the Trojans groaned as they were struck with the sword and the water grew red with blood; then 'as before a dolphin of huge maw other fishes flee and fill the recesses of a harbour of good anchorage, in terror, for it devours whatever it catches', so the Trojans cowered under the banks. The line about the water reddening repeats a line used of earth in the night raid of Book 10 (10.484), with water substituted. Walter Leaf compares the harbour scene on the Hesiodic Shield of Heracles (207 ff.), where silver dolphins hunt fish, and notes that the poet, like most ancients, counts the dolphin as a fish. The image anticipates the closing threat to Lycaon that the fishes will feed on his corpse (21.122-7), and the eels and fish that tear Asteropaeus (21.203-4): in this book the river's creatures become part of the horror.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2 (Books XIII-XXIV), London: Macmillan, 1902, note on 21.20-25

title: Twelve captives as blood-price (poinē) for Patroclus
greek: ποινὴν Πατρόκλοιο Μενοιτιάδαο θανόντος (poinēn Patrokloio Menoitiadao thanontos)
short: Akhilleus takes twelve Trojan youths alive as 'blood-price' (poinē) for Patroclus, fulfilling a vow to kill them at his friend's pyre.
body: At 18.336-7 Akhilleus swore to cut the throats of twelve Trojan youths before Patroclus' pyre; here he takes them, and at 23.175-6 he kills them, an act the narrator calls 'evil deeds'. The word Murray translates 'blood-price' is poinē, the compensation owed for a killing; it is the word used of the dispute over a man's death on the Shield of Akhilleus (18.498). Normally poinē could be paid in goods; Akhilleus turns it into human lives, a sign of how far his grief has moved him beyond the usual rules. The prisoners are 'dazed like fawns' and bound with their own belts; Leaf takes the 'thongs' to be the girdles of their tunics, which shows that they wore no corslets. Leaf also thought these opening lines (1-33) a late addition, inserted to prepare the funeral of Patroclus, and pointed to confusions about which side of the ford Akhilleus is on. Human sacrifice is otherwise almost absent from Homer, which makes this episode stand out sharply.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2 (Books XIII-XXIV), London: Macmillan, 1902, note on 21.28-31; and Introduction to Book XXI, pp. 382-3

title: Lycaon, son of Priam and Laothoe
greek: Λυκάων (Lukaōn)
short: Lycaon had already been captured by Akhilleus once, sold as a slave on Lemnos, ransomed and brought home, only to meet Akhilleus again twelve days later.
body: The narrator gives Lycaon a full back-story before he dies, the device that makes this one of the most moving deaths in the poem. Akhilleus caught him by night in Priam's orchard, cutting young fig shoots to bend into the rail of a chariot. He sold him to Lemnos, where 'the son of Jason' bought him: this is Euneus, son of Jason and Hypsipyle, who supplies the Achaeans with wine (7.467-9) and later gives a silver bowl as Lycaon's price (23.741-7). A 'guest-friend' (xeinos), Eetion of Imbros, ransomed him; Leaf notes that the epithet 'of Imbros' distinguishes this man from Andromache's father Eetion of Thebe. Lycaon escaped from Arisbe to enjoy eleven days at home; 'on the twelfth a god cast him once more into the hands of Achilles'. Leaf judged the allusion to Jason and the Argonaut legend a mark of comparatively late composition, yet praised the episode as one 'of the very highest beauty and pathos'. Akhilleus' amazement that the dead seem to return (21.54-63) is grim irony.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2 (Books XIII-XXIV), London: Macmillan, 1902, note on 21.37-48; and Introduction to Book XXI, p. 382

title: Supplication (hiketeia) on the battlefield
greek: γουνοῦμαί σ', Ἀχιλεῦ· σὺ δέ μ' αἴδεο καί μ' ἐλέησον (gounoumai s', Akhileu; su de m' aideo kai m' eleēson)
short: Lycaon performs the full ritual of supplication, clasping Akhilleus' knees and begging him to feel respect (aidōs) and pity.
body: To supplicate in Greek is literally to 'knee' someone (gounousthai): the suppliant makes himself low and grasps the knees, often also the chin, of the person whose mercy he seeks. In John Gould's classic analysis this physical contact creates a binding claim, protected by Zeus, which the stronger party can accept only by raising the suppliant up. Lycaon's words, 'respect me and have pity', use the two key verbs of the institution, aideomai and eleeō. Lycaon even grips the spear with his other hand, so that the gesture becomes a desperate hold on the weapon itself. Battlefield supplications in the Iliad always fail (Adrestus 6.45-65, Dolon 10.454-7, the sons of Antimachus 11.130-47, Tros 20.463-72), and this one is the most harrowing, because Akhilleus himself tells us that before Patroclus died he used to spare and sell such men (21.100-2; compare 11.104-6). The words 'respect ... and pity' return when Priam supplicates Akhilleus in Book 24 (24.503), and there, at last, supplication succeeds.

sources.cite: John Gould, 'Hiketeia', Journal of Hellenic Studies 93 (1973), 74-103

title: 'The grain of Demeter': a shared meal as a bond
greek: πὰρ γὰρ σοὶ πρώτῳ πασάμην Δημήτερος ἀκτήν (par gar soi prōtōi pasamēn Dēmētēros aktēn)
short: Lycaon claims to be 'as good as a sacred suppliant' because he once ate bread at Akhilleus' table: eating together creates an obligation.
body: 'Demeter's grain' (Dēmētēros aktē) is a solemn way of saying bread. Lycaon argues that because he first tasted bread under Akhilleus' roof, he stands to him 'in place of a reverend suppliant' (anti hiketao aidoioio). Walter Leaf explains the logic: merely to break bread under another man's roof gives a claim to protection even if the host did not intend it, and he compares the Arab custom, reported by William Robertson Smith, that even a thief who has secretly shared a host's drink is safe. Lycaon is not strictly a suppliant who has been accepted, but he claims to be 'as good as' one. He adds an economic argument: he fetched Akhilleus 'the price of a hundred oxen' (Leaf takes this as the value of the silver bowl paid by Euneus, not literal cattle) and has since been ransomed for three times as much, hinting how profitable he would be if sold again. The plea mixes sacred obligation with commerce, the old world of ransom that Akhilleus now rejects.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2 (Books XIII-XXIV), London: Macmillan, 1902, note on 21.75-80

anchor: Nay, friend, do thou too die
title: 'Friend, you too must die': Akhilleus' answer to Lycaon
greek: ἀλλά, φίλος, θάνε καὶ σύ· τίη ὀλοφύρεαι οὕτως; (alla, philos, thane kai su; tiē olophureai houtōs?)
short: Akhilleus refuses mercy, yet calls Lycaon 'friend' and sets his death beside Patroclus' and his own: all men die.
body: This speech is one of the moral centres of the Iliad. Akhilleus explains that before Patroclus died he spared and sold Trojans; now none shall escape. Then the tone changes: 'Nay, friend, die thou too.' Ancient scholars heard mockery in philos ('friend'), a sneer at Lycaon's claim to hospitality; Walter Leaf preferred to hear a sudden, real pity, 'a far finer touch'. Akhilleus places Lycaon's death in a universal frame: Patroclus, a better man, died; Akhilleus himself, handsome, tall, son of a goddess, will die 'at dawn or evening or midday'. Jasper Griffin reads such moments as the heart of Homer's vision of death, in which killer and victim share one mortal condition. The line 'Patroclus also died, who was better far than thou' became proverbial: Plutarch says Callisthenes quoted it to warn Alexander in his glory, and Lucretius adapts it when he reminds the reader that 'good Ancus' died too (De rerum natura 3.1025-6). After this calm, the killing is utterly brutal.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2 (Books XIII-XXIV), London: Macmillan, 1902, note on 21.106-107

anchor: Lie there now among the fishes
title: Denial of burial: Lycaon thrown to the fishes
greek: ἐνταυθοῖ νῦν κεῖσο μετ' ἰχθύσιν (entauthoi nun keiso met' ikhthusin)
short: Akhilleus flings Lycaon's body into the river: no mother will lay him on a bier and lament, and fish will eat his fat.
body: Akhilleus seizes the corpse by the foot and throws it into the river, vaunting that no mother will 'lay thee on a bier and make lament', that is, perform the prothesis and the lament that every Greek funeral required. This is the first of several scenes in Books 21-22 in which he threatens or inflicts the worst fate a Homeric warrior can imagine, the loss of burial, the fear announced already in the proem, where the dead heroes become 'spoil for dogs and birds' (1.4-5). Charles Segal traced how this 'mutilation of the corpse' theme intensifies through the poem until the gods themselves intervene in Book 24. Here the scavengers are fish; with Asteropaeus it will be eels and fishes (21.203-4); with Hector, dogs and birds (22.335-6, 354). Walter Leaf discusses the difficult Greek of 21.126: a fish will dart up to the dark ripple of the surface to eat 'the white fat of Lycaon', and he suspects the passage may be corrupt. The cruelty is also a challenge to the river, which takes offence (21.136).

anchor: single-hooved horses while yet they lived
title: Sacrifices to rivers: bulls and live horses
greek: ζωοὺς δ' ἐν δίνῃσι καθίετε μώνυχας ἵππους (zōous d' en dinēisi kathiete mōnukhas hippous)
short: The Trojans used to honour the Scamander with bulls and by throwing live horses into its eddies; Akhilleus mocks the river's inability to save them.
body: Sacrificing a bull to a river is attested elsewhere in Homer (Nestor sacrifices one to the Alpheus, 11.727-8), and Walter Leaf links it to the common Greek habit of picturing rivers as bulls or bull-headed men; the Scamander itself 'bellows like a bull' at 21.237. Throwing live horses into the water has no other Homeric parallel, and Leaf suggests that Akhilleus names it with contempt as a barbarian custom. There are, however, real parallels: Herodotus says the Persian Magi sacrificed white horses to the river Strymon (7.113), and Pausanias reports that the Argives once drowned horses, bridled, for Poseidon at the spring of Dine (8.7.2). Gregory Nagy points out that the taunt is a pointed insult to the river god: the Trojans have worshipped him for generations, yet he cannot protect them. The insult, together with the corpses choking his stream, explains why Scamander turns against Akhilleus.

title: Asteropaeus, grandson of the river Axius
greek: Ἀστεροπαῖος Πηλεγόνος υἱός (Asteropaios Pēlegonos huios)
short: The Paeonian leader Asteropaeus, grandson of a river god and able to throw with both hands, is the only man in the Iliad who draws Akhilleus' blood.
body: Asteropaeus fights with two spears at once, being 'ambidextrous' (peridexios), and grazes Akhilleus' forearm so that 'the black blood gushed forth', the one time in the poem that Akhilleus is wounded. His name probably recalls asteropē, 'lightning', an irony given Akhilleus' closing boast about Zeus' thunderbolt (21.198-9). Leaf noted several inconsistencies: Asteropaeus says he arrived only eleven days ago, yet he already appears among Troy's allies in Books 12 (12.102) and 17 (17.217, 351); he is missing from the Trojan Catalogue, where a line naming him was later inserted after 2.848; and there the Paeonians are archers 'with curved bows', here spearmen 'with long spears'. Leaf thought the episode a weaker echo of Lycaon's death, its exchange of genealogies modelled on Glaucus and Diomedes (6.145-51), yet he admired its majestic close. Akhilleus' boast that the seed of Zeus outranks the seed of rivers makes the duel a contest of lineages, and helps to provoke the river.

anchor: the water whereof flows the fairest
title: The Axius and Paeonia
greek: Ἀξιοῦ, ὃς κάλλιστον ὕδωρ ἐπὶ γαῖαν ἵησιν (Axiou, hos kalliston hudōr epi gaian hiēsin)
short: The Axius (modern Vardar/Axios) is the great river of Paeonia in Macedonia; ancient readers already doubted Homer's claim that its water was the fairest.
body: Paeonia lay in the Axius valley north of the Thermaic Gulf, 'a land afar' from Troy. The praise of the river's water echoes the Catalogue of Trojan allies (2.849-50), and Walter Leaf thought 21.158 an adaptation of that line. Strabo, who knew the Axius as a muddy river, was puzzled by the praise and argued that the Catalogue line originally referred to a spring called Aia near Amydon, whose clear water flows into the Axius (Strabo, Geography 7, fragment 23). The debate shows that ancient scholars tested Homer's geography against what travellers actually saw, a practice that continues with the springs of Troy in Book 22. Asteropaeus' proud claim to descend from 'wide-flowing Axius' is also a statement of the dignity of river gods, which Akhilleus answers by ranking Zeus above all rivers, Achelous and even Ocean included.

title: Achelous and Ocean, source of all waters
greek: τῷ οὐδὲ κρείων Ἀχελώϊος ἰσοφαρίζει, / οὐδὲ βαθυρρείταο μέγα σθένος Ὠκεανοῖο (tōi oude kreiōn Akhelōios isopharizei, / oude bathurreitao mega sthenos Ōkeanoio)
short: Akhilleus names the mightiest rivers, Achelous and Ocean, to prove that even they fear Zeus; one line about Ocean was missing from some ancient texts.
body: The Achelous, the largest river of mainland Greece, was widely worshipped, and Achelous is named only here in the Iliad. Ocean (Okeanos) is the cosmic river that circles the world and from which, Akhilleus says, 'all rivers flow and every sea, and all the springs and deep wells'; elsewhere Hera calls him 'the origin of the gods' (14.201). Zenodotus omitted line 195 (about Ocean), so that Achelous himself became the source of all waters. Aristarchus kept it, objecting that in Homer Ocean, not Achelous, is the parent of rivers; Leaf sided with him to save 'one of the most majestic lines ever written'. Gregory Nagy argues that both versions are authentic traditional variants, pointing out that Pausanias (8.38.10) quotes the passage without the Ocean line. Even Ocean, Akhilleus concludes, fears Zeus' lightning and thunder. The speech is meant for the listening Scamander, and the river answers it with action.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2 (Books XIII-XXIV), London: Macmillan, 1902, note on 21.194-195

title: Akhilleus' fight with the River (the Battle by the River)
greek: Μάχη παραποτάμιος (Makhē parapotamios); μεμυκὼς ἠΰτε ταῦρος (memukōs ēute tauros)
short: Choked with corpses and insulted, the Scamander attacks Akhilleus with its flood and nearly drowns him: the hero meets a force of nature he cannot defeat.
body: Ancient editors called Book 21 the 'Battle by the River'. The river god first speaks in human form, rebuking Akhilleus because 'beyond men doest deeds of evil' and his stream is choked with dead; then the flood rises, bellowing 'like a bull', and drives Akhilleus in terror across the plain. Gregory Nagy notes that Greek tradition could show a river fighting a hero in animal form (Heracles wrestling Achelous as a bull, in Archilochus); Homer keeps the river elemental, as water itself, while the bull simile nods to the other version. Walter Leaf admired 'the wild grandeur of this splendid scene' but pointed to awkward joins: Akhilleus promises to fight on the plain and then leaps into the river, and Poseidon and Athena's promise of help (21.284-97) has no effect until Hera sends Hephaestus. He took these as signs of an episode added in stages. Thematically, the scene shows Akhilleus' excess turned against him: the killer becomes the hunted, a man who thinks he can master everything is almost swept away.

sources.cite: Gregory Nagy, 'A sampling of comments on Iliad Rhapsody 21', Classical Inquiries (Center for Hellenic Studies, Harvard), 2016, rev. 2018, comment on I.21.200-327
Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2 (Books XIII-XXIV), London: Macmillan, 1902, note on 21.223 and 21.237; and Introduction to Book XXI, pp. 383-4
Archilochus, fragments 286-287 West (Heracles and Achelous)

anchor: a man that guideth its flow
title: The irrigation simile
greek: ὡς δ' ὅτ' ἀνὴρ ὀχετηγὸς ἀπὸ κρήνης μελανύδρου (hōs d' hot' anēr okhetēgos apo krēnēs melanudrou)
short: The flood overtaking Akhilleus is compared to water a gardener lets into his channels, which runs downhill faster than the man can follow.
body: A gardener with a mattock clears the dams in his irrigation channel; the water runs, pebbles rattling, and down a slope it outstrips the man who is guiding it. 'Even thus did the flood of the River ever overtake Achilles ... for the gods are mightier than men.' Walter Leaf notes that irrigation is not otherwise mentioned in Homer (unless in the gardens of Alcinous, Od. 7.129) and calls the simile 'particularly vivid and striking'. Its power lies in contrast. The swiftest of men is likened to a farmer outrun by the trickle he himself released; the terrifying flood is seen through a small, peaceful scene of cultivation. Homer often uses the world of peace in similes to set off the world of war, and here the reversal is precise: a man controls water in the garden, but on the battlefield the water controls the man. The moral, 'gods are mightier than men', anticipates Apollo's words to Akhilleus at the start of Book 22.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2 (Books XIII-XXIV), London: Macmillan, 1902, note on 21.257
Jasper Griffin, Homer on Life and Death, Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1980

title: Akhilleus' death foretold: the arrows of Apollo
greek: λαιψηροῖς ὀλέεσθαι Ἀπόλλωνος βελέεσσιν (laipsērois oleesthai Apollōnos beleessin)
short: Facing drowning, Akhilleus recalls Thetis' prophecy that he would die under the walls of Troy by Apollo's arrows, and wishes Hector had killed him instead.
body: The Iliad never narrates Akhilleus' death, but repeatedly foretells it. His horse Xanthus warns that he will fall 'by a god and a man' (19.416-17); here Thetis' prophecy names Apollo's arrows; and the dying Hector names the killers exactly, 'Paris and Phoebus Apollo ... at the Scaean gate' (22.359-60). The cyclic epic Aethiopis, known from Proclus' summary, told how Akhilleus was killed by Paris and Apollo. Akhilleus' wish that Hector had killed him, so that 'a brave man had been the slayer, and a brave man had he slain', expresses the heroic belief that the worth of a death depends on the killer. Walter Leaf compares Sophocles' Philoctetes (331-6), where Akhilleus' death 'by Phoebus' is reported and a similar thought about noble slayer and noble slain seems to echo this passage. A death by drowning, by contrast, would bring neither glory nor burial.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2 (Books XIII-XXIV), London: Macmillan, 1902, note on 21.278-280
Sophocles, Philoctetes 331-336
Proclus, Chrestomathy, summary of the Aethiopis (death of Achilles)

title: The swineherd boy swept away
greek: ὡς παῖδα συφορβόν, ὅν ῥά τ' ἔναυλος ἀποέρσῃ χειμῶνι περῶντα (hōs paida suphorbon, hon rha t' enaulos apoersēi kheimōni perōnta)
short: Akhilleus fears an ignoble death, like a swineherd boy drowned while crossing a winter torrent: no glory, no burial.
body: The greatest of heroes pictures himself as the humblest of boys, a pig-keeper caught by a mountain torrent (enaulos) in winter. Walter Leaf explains the scene: in autumn swine were driven up to feed on acorns in the oak woods and brought down again as winter came on; he compares Virgil's 'Menalcas came, wet from the winter acorns' (Eclogues 10.20). The point is the kind of death. A warrior killed in battle by a worthy enemy wins kleos and a funeral; drowning is anonymous, and the body may never be found, as the river itself boasts (21.316-23). Odysseus in the storm voices the same fear, wishing he had died at Troy where the Achaeans would have buried him (Od. 5.306-12). The simile measures Akhilleus' terror and the reversal of status that the river has inflicted on him.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, 2nd ed., vol. 2 (Books XIII-XXIV), London: Macmillan, 1902, note on 21.282-283
Virgil, Eclogues 10.20
Homer, Odyssey 5.306-312

title: Scamander's threat: no burial mound for Akhilleus
greek: οὐδέ τί μιν χρεὼ ἔσται τυμβοχόης (oude ti min khreō estai tumbokhoēs)
short: Calling on his brother Simois, the river vows to bury Akhilleus under silt so deep that the Achaeans will never find his bones or raise his mound.
body: Scamander summons his brother river Simois ('Dear brother') to help, and imagines Akhilleus' fine armour lying under slime and his body under 'shingle past all measuring': 'Even here shall be his sepulchre, nor shall he have need of a heaped-up mound.' The rare word tumbokhoē, 'heaping of a mound', divided ancient critics: Crates read it as a noun, Aristarchus as an infinitive; Walter Leaf thought Aristarchus wrong. Leaf also notes the possibility of a cenotaph, a funeral monument without a body, which Homer never describes but hints at when Andromache burns Hector's clothes (22.510-14). The threat strikes at the heart of heroic hopes. A mound (tumbos, sēma) preserves a hero's name, as Hector boasts in Book 7 (7.86-91), and the Odyssey later describes the great tomb of Akhilleus and Patroclus on the Hellespont (Od. 24.80-4). The river would deny Akhilleus even the memorial that makes kleos visible.

title: Hephaestus 'Crook-foot' (Kullopodiōn): fire against water
greek: κυλλοπόδιον (kullopodion)
short: Hera calls her lame son Hephaestus, god of fire, to fight the river: the battle becomes a cosmic conflict of fire and water.
body: Kullopodiōn, 'crook-footed', refers to Hephaestus' lameness, which the Iliad explains in two ways: Zeus hurled him from Olympus (1.590-4), or Hera threw him out at birth (18.395-7). An ancient critic thought it unseemly for Hera to mention her son's deformity when asking a favour, and a note in the scholia marks the line as rejected; Walter Leaf suspects a scribal confusion and calls the line 'obviously indispensable'. Hera's words, 'it was against thee that we deemed eddying Xanthus to be matched in fight', recall the pairing of opposed gods at 20.73-4. What follows is an elemental battle: Hephaestus burns the dead on the plain, then the elms, willows and tamarisks, then the river itself until its waters boil. Gregory Nagy describes the clash as a cosmic conflict between fire and water, in which fire wins; ancient allegorists read the whole battle of the gods in this elemental way (see the Theomachy note).

title: The cauldron simile
greek: ὡς δὲ λέβης ζεῖ ἔνδον ἐπειγόμενος πυρὶ πολλῷ (hōs de lebēs zei endon epeigomenos puri pollōi)
short: The burning river seethes like a cauldron rendering down the fat of a hog over a fierce fire of dry sticks.
body: The river god, a few moments ago a terrifying flood, is reduced to a pot on the kitchen fire. The simile is homely and exact: the cauldron bubbles 'in every part' as it melts the lard of a fattened hog, with dry faggots heaped underneath. Walter Leaf reports Aristarchus' observation that Homer never shows his heroes boiling meat (they roast it), and notes that strictly the simile describes melting fat, not boiling flesh; the poet knows the cauldron from everyday life even if heroes do not use it so. The comparison turns the elemental struggle of fire and water into something almost comic, which prepares for the burlesque battle of the gods that follows. The river's surrender is equally domestic: he appeals to Hera, mother of his attacker, and swears never again to help the Trojans, 'not when all Troy shall burn', a forward glance to the city's destruction.

title: The Theomachy (battle of the gods)
greek: ἀμφὶ δὲ σάλπιγξεν μέγας οὐρανός (amphi de salpinxen megas ouranos)
short: The gods clash, heaven rings 'as with a trumpet', and Zeus laughs at the sight. Critics have found the scene sublime, absurd, or allegorical.
body: The battle of the gods promised in Book 20 finally happens. The line about heaven trumpeting was admired by 'Longinus', who quotes it with 20.61-5 as an example of sublimity, yet in the next breath calls the episode impious 'unless perhaps it is to be taken allegorically' (On the Sublime 9.6-7). That allegorical reading is very old: Theagenes of Rhegium (6th century BC) already explained the gods' battle as a conflict of natural elements and moral qualities. Walter Leaf, by contrast, called the Theomachy 'a ridiculous harlequinade', perhaps an early parody, and Aristarchus noted that the trumpet appears only in metaphor and simile, never as an instrument of Homeric battle. Zeus 'laughed aloud in joy' to see the gods fight; Leaf observes that only here and at 21.508 does Homer's Zeus go beyond a smile. Gregory Nagy calls the scene 'divine burlesque' and, citing Walter Burkert, stresses that such comic treatment of the gods is archaizing rather than new, with Near Eastern parallels. The contrast with the deadly human battle is surely intended: gods' quarrels end in tears and laughter, men's in death.

title: 'Dog-fly' (kunamuia)
greek: κυνάμυια (kunamuia)
short: Ares insults Athena, and Hera insults Aphrodite, as 'dog-fly': a compound combining the shamelessness of a dog with the impudence of a fly.
body: Kunamuia, 'dog-fly', is used twice in this book (Ares of Athena, Hera of Aphrodite) and nowhere else in Homer. The ancient explanation is that it joins two proverbial creatures: the dog stands for shamelessness (compare Akhilleus' insult 'dog-face', 1.225) and the fly for persistent boldness (Athena gives Menelaus 'the daring of a fly' at 17.570). Walter Leaf notes that such double-noun compounds have almost no parallel in Homer. Ares' grievance is old: in Book 5 Athena guided Diomedes' spear into his belly (5.855-61). The quarrel is played for laughs. Ares strikes the aegis, which even Zeus' lightning cannot pierce; Athena flattens him with a boundary stone and laughs; Aphrodite, leading him away, is knocked down by a blow to the breast. The insults show the gods behaving like quarrelsome mortals, the 'divine burlesque' of this part of the book.

title: The boundary stone and Ares' giant fall
greek: τόν ῥ' ἄνδρες πρότεροι θέσαν ἔμμεναι οὖρον ἀρούρης (ton rh' andres proteroi thesan emmenai ouron arourēs)
short: Athena fells Ares with an ancient boundary stone; the war god sprawls over 'seven roods' (plethra), a rare picture of divine giantism.
body: Athena's weapon is a black, jagged stone 'that men of former days had set to be the boundary mark of a field'. Boundary stones (ouroi) were sacred and ancient; a simile in Book 12 shows two men quarrelling over boundary markers in a common field (12.421-4). There is quiet irony in the goddess of wisdom using a marker of settled agricultural order to fell the god of disorder. Ares falls and covers 'seven roods', in Greek seven plethra; a plethron is about thirty metres, so the god stretches over some two hundred metres. Walter Leaf notes that Homer's gods are 'divinely tall' but rarely monstrous; the only comparable images are the giant Tityos covering nine plethra in the Underworld (Od. 11.577) and the vast shout of the wounded Ares in Book 5 (5.859-61), all of them, he thinks, in later passages. Athena's taunt, 'Fool' (nēpie), is a recurrent form of address in this book.

anchor: the Avengers invoked of thy mother
title: The Erinyes of a mother
greek: μητρὸς ἐρινύας (mētros erinuas)
short: Athena tells Ares that his fall pays off his mother Hera's curses, because he deserted the Achaeans for the Trojans.
body: Murray's 'Avengers' are the Erinyes, the powers that punish wrongs done to parents, guests and the order of the world. Here Hera's Erinyes fall on her son because he broke a promise: in Book 5 Athena complains that Ares had pledged to fight for the Achaeans but went over to the Trojans (5.832-4). Walter Leaf thinks the word here means little more than 'curses' and has lost its full moral force; he compares the Odyssey's 'the Erinyes of a mother' who pursue Oedipus (Od. 11.280) and Aeschylus' Eumenides, where the Erinyes call themselves 'Curses' (Arai, Eum. 417). Elsewhere in the Iliad the Erinyes enforce the curses of Phoenix's father (9.454) and of Meleager's mother (9.571), and they even silence Akhilleus' talking horse (19.418). Applied to a quarrel among gods, the solemn idea becomes part of the comedy.

title: Poseidon and Apollo in the service of Laomedon
greek: Λαομέδοντι ἀγήνορι θητεύσαμεν εἰς ἐνιαυτὸν μισθῷ ἔπι ῥητῷ (Laomedonti agēnori thēteusamen eis eniauton misthōi epi rhētōi)
short: Poseidon reminds Apollo that they once worked a year for wages for the Trojan king Laomedon, who cheated them and threatened them: why help his people?
body: Poseidon tells the story of the gods' humiliation: at Zeus' bidding they served Priam's father Laomedon for a year as hired labourers (thētes), Poseidon building the wall of Troy and Apollo herding cattle on Ida. When the term ended, Laomedon refused payment and threatened to bind them, sell them overseas and lop off their ears. Walter Leaf notes that the same legend appears at 7.452-3, where both gods build the wall, a discrepancy that was one reason for Aristarchus' rejection of that passage; Homer gives no reason for the servitude. The word thēteuein implies hired service, the lowest status a free man could have. Horace remembers the story: Laomedon 'cheated the gods of their agreed wage' (Odes 3.3.21-2). Laomedon also cheated Heracles, who then sacked Troy (5.640-2; Apollodorus 2.5.9). The episode explains Poseidon's hatred of Troy and explains why the walls of Troy, on whose 'divine' tower (theios pyrgos, 21.526) Priam now stands watching Akhilleus, are called the work of gods.

title: Apollo: mortals are like leaves
greek: δειλῶν, οἳ φύλλοισιν ἐοικότες ἄλλοτε μέν τε ζαφλεγέες τελέθουσιν (deilōn, hoi phulloisin eoikotes allote men te zaphlegees telethousin)
short: Apollo refuses to fight Poseidon over 'pitiful mortals' who flourish and wither like leaves, recalling Glaucus' famous simile in Book 6.
body: Apollo declines the challenge: he would be mad to fight 'for the sake of mortals, pitiful creatures, that like unto leaves are now full of flaming life, eating the fruit of the field, and now again pine away and perish'. The image recalls Glaucus' words to Diomedes, 'as are the generations of leaves, so are those of men' (6.146-9), and was taken up by the lyric poet Mimnermus (fr. 2 West). Walter Leaf thought the mixture of metaphors here ('full of fire' yet 'eating the fruit of the earth') so awkward that it might be deliberate. But the reasoning matters: from the gods' height, the human war is not worth a quarrel, and Apollo also feels shame (aidōs) at striking his father's brother. Hera has just said the same: it is not seemly to hurt an immortal 'for mortals' sake' (21.379-80). Jasper Griffin argues that such moments define the gods' ease against the seriousness of human suffering.

title: Artemis 'Mistress of Animals' (potnia thērōn)
greek: πότνια θηρῶν, Ἄρτεμις ἀγροτέρη (potnia thērōn, Artemis agroterē)
short: Artemis is called 'queen of wild beasts' and 'of the wild wood': titles of an ancient goddess who rules animals and the hunt.
body: Potnia thērōn, 'lady of wild beasts', occurs only here in Homer, and agroterē means 'of the wild countryside'. The title belongs to a very old religious type: images of a goddess holding or flanked by animals appear in Near Eastern, Minoan and archaic Greek art (a winged 'mistress of animals' decorates the handles of the François Vase), and Walter Burkert treats Artemis as the Greek heir of this figure, mistress of the hunt and of the wild places outside the city. The grand title is followed by humiliation. Artemis rebukes her brother for cowardice and is beaten about the ears by Hera with her own bow, then runs weeping to Zeus. The gap between the cult title and the comic action is typical of the Theomachy, which treats the gods with a lightness unthinkable in their worship.

title: Artemis, a 'lion to women': goddess of sudden death
greek: ἐπεί σε λέοντα γυναιξὶ Ζεὺς θῆκεν (epei se leonta gunaixi Zeus thēken)
short: Hera mocks Artemis as a lion only against women, alluding to her role as bringer of sudden death to women with her arrows.
body: In Homer the 'gentle arrows' of Artemis bring sudden, painless death to women, as those of Apollo do to men: Artemis killed Andromache's mother (6.428) and Laodameia (6.205), and in the Odyssey Odysseus asks his mother whether Artemis' arrows killed her (Od. 11.172-3). Hera's taunt turns this power into an insult: Zeus made you a lion against women, so go and kill deer on the mountains instead of fighting your betters. Walter Leaf notes that Homer has no feminine word for lioness, and suggests a connection with the Semitic image of death as a lion; he adds that Artemis was said to have been worshipped in the form of a lioness at Ambracia. Hera then disarms her and beats her with her own bow. Leaf observes that the scene that follows, with Artemis weeping on her father's knees, is closely modelled on Aphrodite's complaint to Dione and Zeus in Book 5 (5.370-417), with two lines repeated exactly (21.509-10 = 5.373-4).

title: Artemis as a dove fleeing a falcon
greek: ὥς τε πέλεια, ἥ ῥά θ' ὑπ' ἴρηκος κοίλην εἰσέπτατο πέτρην (hōs te peleia, hē rha th' hup' irēkos koilēn eiseptato petrēn)
short: The huntress flees like a dove from a falcon into a cleft rock, 'nor is it her lot to be taken'; the same image returns, fatally, for Hector.
body: The hunting goddess becomes the hunted bird, a neat comic reversal. But the simile also carries a careful qualification: the dove escapes into a hollow rock, 'nor is it her lot to be taken' (oud' ara hoi ge halōmenai aisimon ēen). A goddess cannot be destroyed. In Book 22 the same pair of birds returns with deadly force: Akhilleus swoops on Hector 'as a falcon in the mountains ... after a trembling dove' (22.139-44), and Hector has no cleft to fly into, for his death is fated. Reading the two similes together shows how Homer uses repeated images across books: what is play among immortals is doom among men. The word Murray renders 'cleft' (khēramos) occurs only here in Homer, as Walter Leaf notes.

title: 'Beyond fate' (huper moron)
greek: μὴ Δαναοὶ πέρσειαν ὑπὲρ μόρον ἤματι κείνῳ (mē Danaoi perseian huper moron ēmati keinōi)
short: Apollo enters Troy lest the Greeks sack it 'beyond fate' that day: Homer imagines events that could, but must not, overrun what is destined.
body: Moira or moros is a person's or a city's allotted portion, above all the share of death. Troy is fated to fall, but not on this day and not to Akhilleus. The idea of something happening 'beyond fate' recurs at critical moments: Zeus fears that Akhilleus might storm the wall 'beyond fate' (20.30), the Achaeans almost sail home 'beyond fate' in Book 2 (2.155), and in the Odyssey Zeus complains that men bring suffering on themselves 'beyond their portion' (Od. 1.34-5). Scholars disagree on how literally to take this. Walter Leaf observes that such phrases are never used of anything that actually happens; they apply to the future or to unrealized possibilities in the past, so that the poet can say what would have occurred but for divine intervention. Whatever one makes of fate, the gods act here as guardians of the plot: Apollo's next move, deceiving Akhilleus in Agenor's shape, is what keeps Troy standing.

title: Smoke from a burning city
greek: ὡς δ' ὅτε καπνὸς ἰὼν εἰς οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἵκηται ἄστεος αἰθομένοιο, θεῶν δέ ἑ μῆνις ἀνῆκε (hōs d' hote kapnos iōn eis ouranon eurun hikētai asteos aithomenoio, theōn de he mēnis anēke)
short: Akhilleus' slaughter is likened to smoke rising from a city burned by the gods' wrath: an image that looks ahead to the fall of Troy.
body: The gods have gone back to Olympus; on earth Akhilleus keeps killing. The simile compares the toil and grief he causes to the smoke of a burning city, driven by 'the wrath of the gods' (theōn mēnis). The word mēnis is the first word of the Iliad, Akhilleus' 'wrath'; here it is the gods' anger, and the burning city is an unmistakable foreshadowing of Troy's fate, which the river has just foreseen ('when all Troy shall burn', 21.375). Walter Leaf criticised the logic, since strictly the deeds of Akhilleus are compared to the smoke rather than to the fire, and he notes that the simile adapts one in Book 18 (18.207-14), where Akhilleus' blazing head is compared to signal fires on a besieged island. Read as poetry rather than logic, the image fuses Akhilleus' wrath with divine wrath, and his rampage with the destruction that awaits the city.

title: Agenor's stand: a rehearsal for Hector
greek: Ἀγήνωρ Ἀντήνορος υἱός (Agēnōr Antēnoros huios)
short: Agenor debates with himself, decides to face Akhilleus, is saved by Apollo, and Apollo in his likeness lures Akhilleus away so the Trojans reach the city.
body: Agenor's name means 'manly'. His soliloquy, opening 'Ah, woe is me', is built on the same plan as Hector's in Book 22: Walter Leaf shows that both men reject flight, consider a roundabout escape, dismiss it with the line 'But why doth my heart thus hold converse with me?', and choose to fight with faint hope. Agenor reasons that Akhilleus too 'has but one life' and can be pierced by bronze; Leaf notes that Akhilleus' invulnerability is a post-Homeric legend. Agenor then stands 'as a pard' (leopard) that, even when speared, will not stop until it grapples with the hunter or dies. His spear strikes Akhilleus' greave without piercing it. Apollo snatches him away in mist and, taking Agenor's form, draws Akhilleus off towards the river while the routed Trojans pour into the city. The episode delays the climax, lets the poet try out Hector's decision on a lesser man, and prepares Apollo's taunt at the opening of Book 22.

title: Akhilleus' greave of tin, 'the gift of the god'
greek: κνημὶς νεοτεύκτου κασσιτέροιο (knēmis neoteuktou kassiteroio)
short: Agenor's spear rings off Akhilleus' new greave, made of tin by Hephaestus; divine armour, not a magic body, protects the Homeric Akhilleus.
body: Greaves (knēmides) protected the shins. Hephaestus made Akhilleus' new greaves of 'pliant tin' (18.612-13), a soft metal that would be useless in real life but marks the armour as divine and precious. Agenor's spear 'leapt back' and 'the gift of the god stayed it'; the same phrase is used of the gold layer that stopped Asteropaeus' spear (21.165). Walter Leaf suspected line 594 of being added to allude to the making of the arms in Book 18. The scene matters for the legend of Akhilleus. In Homer he is protected by his armour and by the gods, and his body can be wounded, as Asteropaeus shows (21.166-8). The famous story of his invulnerable body and vulnerable heel is later: Leaf notes that invulnerability is 'a purely post-Homeric legend', and the dipping in the Styx is first attested in Statius' Achilleid in the first century AD (1.133-4).
